replies:
You don't have a resume on file here yet. Paste your resume (or paste the Experience, Skills and Education sections) and I'll read it and save every line as draft facts.
If you want a quick checklist now of common gaps I look for on resumes for Junior Software Engineer roles, here are the top things to check and typical fixes:
1. Concrete projects (3+), each with: one-sentence goal, your role, tech stack, and measurable result or outcome (users, performance, tests, PRs merged). Fix: add bullets like "Built X using React and Node; reduced page load by 30% for 5k users."
2. Clear skills section separated by: Languages, Frameworks/Libraries, Tools (Git, CI), and Concepts (algorithms, OOP, databases). Fix: order by relevance to the job and avoid vague buzzwords.
3. Link to code (GitHub) and at least one runnable demo or deployed app (link). Fix: add repo links to project lines; ensure README explains how to run.
4. Evidence of CS fundamentals: algorithms/data-structures, complexity, system design basics. Fix: list courses, competitions, or mention interview prep.
5. Internship, part-time, or open-source contributions with specifics (PR count, issues fixed). Fix: include contribution stats and link to PRs.
6. Tests and CI: mention unit/integration tests and CI pipelines if you used them. Fix: "Wrote 120 unit tests with Jest; CI via GitHub Actions runs on each PR."
7. Impact and numbers: where possible, add metrics (reduced latency X ms, handled Y users, increased test coverage to Z%). Fix: quantify results.
8. Education and relevant coursework or certifications (CS degree, bootcamp, MOOCs). Fix: include graduation year, GPA only if strong, relevant courses.
9. Resume length/format: one page, consistent verb tense, no personal pronouns, easy-to-scan bullets. Fix: trim nontechnical roles to 1–2 bullets emphasizing transferable skills.
10. Tailoring: for each application, mirror job posting keywords and list the most relevant projects/skills first. Fix: have 2–3 resume variants (web, backend, full-stack).
Paste your resume now and I will:
- save every entry as draft facts,
- then give a 2–3 line summary (latest role, top skills, education),
- list 2–3 specific, prioritized changes to make it stronger for Junior Software Engineer roles,
- and offer to search for matching jobs.

Good — final round prep for Lincoln International analyst. I’ll give a short company/role brief, top questions they’ll ask, sample answers you can adapt (behavioral + technical/financial), three concrete things to practice live, and a 10‑point checklist for the day-of. I’ll assume the interview is 60–90 minutes with senior bankers and a case or modeling test; tell me if that’s wrong.
Company + role brief (what to know, briefly)
- Lincoln International: middle‑market M&A and advisory, deal‑focused, client service across sell‑side/buy‑side, industry teams. Expect focus on transaction experience, deal process understanding, modeling and attention to detail, and cultural fit for a small, collaborative team.
- Analyst role: execution-heavy—financial modeling, transaction due diligence, pitchbook prep, and long hours. They want technical accuracy, professionalism, and evidence you can support senior bankers and interact with clients/clients’ advisors.
Top questions they’ll ask (with what they want)
1) "Walk me through your résumé / this deal." — They want structured storytelling, your role, concrete contributions, and results.
2) Behavioral: "Tell me about a time you missed a deadline / made a mistake." — They want ownership, remediation, and what you changed.
3) Technical accounting/valuation: "How do you value a company? Walk me through DCF." — They want correct steps, assumptions, and sensitivity to drivers.
4) Modeling test / case questions: "Explain your assumptions; why is EBITDA the focus?" — They want clear logic, speed, and spreadsheet thinking.
5) Fit: "Why Lincoln? Why this industry?" — They want specifics: deal examples, culture fit, and career trajectory.
6) Market/sector: "What’s happening in [industry] M&A right now?" — They want concise, current drivers and implications for deal flow.
7) Stress/pressure: "Tell me about a time you worked 12+ hours to finish something." — They want endurance plus how you sustain quality.
Two short behavioral scripts you can use (STAR, ready to speak)
1) Résumé/deal pitch (60–90 seconds)
- Situation: [Company X was exploring a strategic sale / raised growth capital].
- Task: My role was analyst supporting the sell‑side process: build financial model, prepare CIM and comps, and coordinate diligence documents.
- Action: I built a 3‑statement model with monthly-to-quarterly adjustments, ran comps and precedent M&A, prepared 10 slides for the CIM highlighting revenue drivers, and tracked buyer questions via a shared diligence tracker. I flagged an accounting treatment that inflated near‑term EBITDA, and adjusted projections with the CFO.
- Result: We shortened the data-room Q&A cycle by 30%, delivered cleaner forecasts that buyers relied on, and the company closed at [if you have a number, insert it; otherwise say “a premium to initial expectations”].
(Practice delivering in 60s. Swap facts you actually did.)
2) Mistake/learning (45–60 seconds)
- Situation: I mis-tagged revenue timing in a model before a deadline.
- Task: Fix the model and notify the team.
- Action: I immediately traced the error, corrected the timing, reran outputs, informed lead and provided a clean version, and created a checklist to prevent recurrence.
- Result: No client impact; team adopted my checklist and similar errors dropped. I learned speed + double‑check steps under pressure.
Two technical answers to memorize (short, precise)
1) DCF, in bullets you can say aloud
- Project unlevered free cash flow for 5–7 years (NOPAT → add depreciation → capex & working capital changes).
- Discount at WACC to get enterprise value; add non‑operating assets, subtract debt to get equity value.
- Use terminal value (Gordon growth or exit multiple); run sensitivities on WACC and terminal multiple.
- Key point to state: show how revenue growth, margins, capex and working capital shape FCF — and why sensitivity matters.
2) LBO basics they might test
- Use purchase price, implied equity check; model debt tranches and interest schedule; project operating cash flows to pay down debt; compute IRR and multiple on equity at exit.
- Key levers: entry multiple, exit multiple, leverage, margin improvement, and revenue growth cadence.
Three focused live-practice drills (do these out loud)
1) 60‑second walk-through of your top deal. Time it, record if possible, tighten to 45–60s.
2) Mock DCF explanation in 90 seconds, then answer a follow-up: "If revenue falls 20%, what happens to value?" Work numbers quickly.
3) Short behavioral Q/A: pick 3 tough questions (conflict, mistake, leadership) and practice concise STAR answers.
10-point day-of checklist (exact actions)
1) Bring a hard copy résumé and your printed deal one-pager (one page: role, deliverables, results).
2) Review your top 2 deals and memorize your exact contributions and numbers.
3) Re-run quick mental DCF and comps steps; have definitions ready (NOPAT, WACC, EBITDA adjustments).
4) Prepare 3 insightful questions for interviewers: 1 about a recent Lincoln deal you read, 1 about team structure/expectations for analysts, 1 about development path.
5) One-liner on "Why Lincoln?" tied to a specific recent deal or the middle‑market focus.
6) Plan to start with a brief professional greeting + 2-sentence pitch of your background (30s).
7) Organize travel, logins, and contact details; be 10–15 minutes early.
8) If case/modeling test: use clear assumptions, show work, and explain choices aloud.
9) Send a concise thank-you note within 24 hours (I can draft it; say who you met).
10) Sleep, hydrate, and review cheat‑sheet (one page) with bullets: top deal facts, formulas, and key questions.

Common gaps I’ll watch for in your answers
- Too long: keep answers structured and concise (45–90s).
- Lack of numbers: include percentages, timelines, and outcomes where possible.
- Weak ownership: show what you did specifically, not team-level.
Next step
Tell me (one thing): do you want a timed mock interview now (I’ll ask the first question) or a customized thank‑you draft after your final? If mock, say "mock now" and I’ll ask the first question.
